sysd-found-101.title: DNS: the phone book of the Internet
sysd-found-101.text:
Computers find each other by number, but people remember names. The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates the names people use into the numeric IP addresses that computers use. It works like the phone book of the Internet: www.example.com translates to 93.184.216.34 in IPv4 and to a much longer address in IPv6.

No single store holds all of this. Responsibility for each domain goes to its own authoritative servers, and administrators can hand pieces of a name to other servers. The result is a distributed, fault-tolerant service designed to avoid one large central store, and it can serve billions of hosts efficiently. It also mirrors how the Internet is run: each piece of a name is a zone of administrative autonomy, delegated to a manager.

A name server keeps the records for a domain and answers queries against them. Those records are conventionally kept in a structured text file called a zone file. Because records can be updated quickly, a service can change its network location while users keep typing the same hostname.

Queries run on port 53 over UDP and TCP. DNS began with UDP alone; reliability, security and privacy concerns later brought TCP and other transports. DNS also stores more than addresses. It has been extended to hold signing records, which {{ref:sysd-found-195}} explains, and, as a general-purpose store, spam blocklists.

sysd-found-201.title: Anycast: one address, many servers
sysd-found-201.text:
Anycast gives one IP address to servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one. Each server announces the shared address by BGP, the protocol routers use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. Routers treat the announcements as alternative routes and often pick the path with fewer hops.

All Internet root name servers use anycast. Many commercial DNS providers switched to it for faster queries, resilience and spread-out load. An early worry was that a long-lived TCP connection could be rerouted to another server midway. In practice this was not observed, and measured failures from instance switches were below 0.017%.

The sharp edge is failure. If a dead server keeps announcing its route, it becomes a black hole for the nearby clients, the most serious failure mode. The automation that withdraws routes can itself fail. And anyone whose announcements are accepted can hijack anycast traffic, so announcements must be filtered.

sysd-found-114.title: How DNS queries travel: UDP, TCP and encrypted transports
sysd-found-114.text:
Classic DNS is startlingly plain. A client sends a clear-text request in a single UDP packet to port 53 and gets a clear-text reply in a single UDP packet. With EDNS support, answers longer than 512 bytes may use larger UDP packets. UDP suits a simple query-response protocol, and TCP's complexity can burden a server that answers simple requests from huge numbers of clients.

Still, UDP is limited by its lack of transport-layer encryption, a way to verify who is talking and reliable delivery, and by message length. RFC 1123, in 1989, added optional TCP, which allows longer responses, reliable delivery and reuse of long-lived connections.

Encrypted transports came later. DNS over TLS, or DoT (2016), protects the entire connection with TLS on TCP port 853. Its standard, RFC 7858, supports opportunistic and authenticated encryption but did not make it mandatory for server or client to authenticate. DoH (2018) is DNS carried over {{ref:sysd-found-048}}. It tunnels queries over TCP port 443, so it looks like web traffic, though the two are easily told apart without proper padding.

DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, 2022) has privacy properties similar to DoT and latency similar to classic DNS over UDP. DNSCrypt (2011), developed outside the IETF, has clients encrypt query payloads with servers' public keys published in the DNS, and uses TCP or UDP port 443.

sysd-found-102.title: Reading a domain name as a tree
sysd-found-102.text:
Read a domain name from right to left and you are walking down a tree. The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each carry a label and zero or more records of information about that name. A full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots, so www.example.com is www joined to example.com. The rightmost label, here com, is the TLD, introduced in {{ref:sysd-found-202}}.

Each label names a subdivision of the domain to its right, and the tree may have up to 127 levels. A label may hold up to 63 characters, and a whole name may not exceed 253 characters in text form. Hostname labels use only letters, digits and hyphens, cannot start or end with a hyphen, and ignore case. To show other alphabets, browsers use IDNA, which maps Unicode strings into that character set with Punycode.

The tree divides into zones beginning at the root zone, and a zone may contain as many domains as its manager chooses.

sysd-found-202.title: Top-level domains: the last label of every name
sysd-found-202.text:
Made-up internal names can collide with real ones later. ICANN rejected .home and .corp as TLDs over conflicts with networks already using them, and local domains such as test.dev collided with the .dev TLD created in 2019.

A top-level domain, or TLD, is the highest level of the DNS hierarchy below the root: the last label of any name, such as .com in www.example.com. TLD names are installed in the root zone. ICANN delegates management of most of them to specific organizations and operates IANA, which maintains the root zone.

IANA sorts TLDs into infrastructure, generic, generic restricted, sponsored, country-code and internationalized country-code types. Country-code names are two letters that, with some historical exceptions, match the territory's two-letter ISO 3166 code. The IETF also reserves names such as .test, .local and .onion, which should not be used in production on the global DNS.

sysd-found-203.title: Time to live: giving data an expiry
sysd-found-203.text: Data that lives forever can cause trouble, so networks give it an expiry. A TTL is a counter or timestamp attached to data; when the count or time runs out, the data is discarded or revalidated. In IP, it is an 8-bit header field with a maximum of 255, reduced by every router. At zero the datagram is discarded, which stops packets circulating forever. IPv4 defines it in seconds, but in practice it falls by one per hop, so IPv6 renamed it the hop limit. In DNS, the authoritative server sets a TTL per record to tell resolvers how long to keep it.

sysd-found-109.title: Resource records: the entries DNS stores
sysd-found-109.text: Everything DNS knows is stored as resource records. On the wire, each has NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA fields. TYPE gives the format and use of the data, and RDATA holds the type-specific part, such as an address or an MX priority and hostname. CLASS is IN for ordinary Internet records. The TTL counts the seconds the record stays valid, up to 2^31 minus 1, about 68 years. Records of the same type form a set, an RRset, which resolvers return whole.

sysd-found-117.title: Who hands out domain names: registrars and registries
sysd-found-117.text: What a buyer gets from a domain name is the right to use it. That right is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the master records of names for each TLD. The registrant, the person or organization that asked for the name, is a customer of the registrar, sometimes through resellers. The registry takes registration information from registrars and publishes it using the WHOIS protocol. Most gTLD registries have kept that data centrally since about 2001, a thick approach, while COM and NET use a thin one that keeps only basic data.

sysd-found-118.title: Before DNS: one file called HOSTS.TXT
sysd-found-118.text: Before DNS, the address book of an entire network was a single file. HOSTS.TXT, kept by the Network Information Center (NIC), mapped host names to the numerical addresses of ARPANET computers, and every host fetched it by FTP. The bandwidth needed to distribute each new version grew with the square of the number of hosts. Local organizations ran their own names but had to wait for the NIC to change the file. By the early 1980s the central table was slow and unwieldy. Paul Mockapetris created DNS in 1983, and RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 superseded the original specifications in November 1987.

sysd-found-110.title: DNS record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS and friends
sysd-found-110.text:
A domain publishes several kinds of information, and each kind has its own record type. An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record does the same for an IPv6 address. Both are essential for turning names into IP addresses. A CNAME record aliases one name to another, often pointing child names at the main domain. It forwards to the other name and does not itself provide an IP address.

Other types point elsewhere. Records of type MX direct email to the right mail server, which also protects mail delivery against failures and spreads its load. An NS record names the authoritative DNS servers for a domain and directs queries to them for further lookups. A PTR record maps an IP address back to a domain name and is commonly used to verify the authenticity of a server.

An SRV record specifies a host and port for services such as VoIP, voice calls over IP, and is used together with A records. A TXT record attaches human-readable text to a domain, for example verification records such as SPF for email security. The SOA, or start of authority, record stores administrative information and is among the most common types.

sysd-found-111.title: Reverse DNS lookup: from address back to name
sysd-found-111.text: Sometimes you know the address and want the name. A reverse lookup asks the DNS for the domain names tied to an IP address that is already known. The answers are PTR records under the infrastructure TLD arpa, with the address written in reverse order, so 208.80.152.2 becomes 2.152.80.208.in-addr.arpa. Without a PTR record the lookup cannot resolve, and several names may share one IP address. Email servers commonly use reverse lookups to check that a message came from a valid server, and many reject messages from servers that do not support them.

sysd-found-126.title: CNAME records: one name standing in for another
sysd-found-126.text: A resource often has several names: one canonical, or primary, name and some aliases. A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and names the canonical one, but provides no IP address itself. If a node has a CNAME record it should hold no other data, so an alias and its canonical name cannot differ. A server that finds a CNAME instead of the wanted record includes it in the response and restarts the query at the canonical name. Records that point at another name should use the primary name, not an alias, and software should follow CNAME chains and signal CNAME loops as an error.

sysd-found-204.title: The rarer DNS records: DNAME, SVCB, CAA, TLSA and more
sysd-found-204.text:
Beyond A, AAAA, MX and NS, DNS defines many more record types for aliases, locating services, certificates, security and zone transfers. A DNAME record aliases a name and all its subnames, unlike CNAME, which aliases only the exact name. Non-standard ALIAS or ANAME records synthesize A and AAAA records from a target so the bare domain can be aliased. TXT began as human-readable text but since the early 1990s mostly carries machine-readable data such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC. SRV gives generalized service location for newer protocols, instead of protocol-specific records like MX.

SVCB records give clients connection metadata such as supported protocols and alternative endpoints. The record type named for {{ref:sysd-found-048}} is a specialized SVCB that supplies those connection details up front, enabling Encrypted Client Hello and lower first-connection latency. CAA constrains which certificate authorities may issue for a domain. TLSA associates a TLS server certificate or key with a name for DANE, and SSHFP publishes SSH host key fingerprints.

Five types belong to signing, which {{ref:sysd-found-195}} explains. RRSIG holds signatures and DNSKEY the zone key. DS identifies a delegated zone's signing key. NSEC proves a name does not exist, and NSEC3 proves it without letting anyone list the zone's names.

Some types serve the protocol itself. AXFR transfers a whole zone from primary to secondary, and IXFR only the differences since a serial number. ANY returns all cached records, and OPT supports EDNS. Many early types are obsolete: MX replaced MD and MF, and HINFO is now repurposed for minimal answers to ANY queries.

sysd-found-121.title: The three parts of DNS
sysd-found-121.text: DNS has three major components: the domain name space with its resource records, the name servers that hold the data, and the resolvers that extract it for clients. A name server has complete information about a subset of the space, for which it is the authority, plus pointers to other servers. A resolver answers client requests directly or follows referrals. It is typically a system routine, so no protocol is needed between it and the user program. To the user, DNS is a call to a local resolver; to a name server, it is zones to refresh from master copies while answering queries.
